In 1975, the national average load factor, as measured by the weighted average load factors of systems in the nine regional council areas, was 62.3 percent. The load factor for the Southeast Regional Council area was 60.6 percent. During the same period, the load factor of the Duke Power Company was 61.7 percent which indicates that, other things being equal, the potential savings to Duke Power from measures to flatten load may be somewhat less than for systems elsewhere in the SERC area.
It is, of course, recognized that certain valley periods that occur annually in a load curve such as that of the Duke Power Company must necessarily be used for maintenance requirements and hydro reservoir filling. If the load curve is flattened to the maximum, maintenance of generating facilities would still have to be scheduled. This would increase the percentage of reserve system capability required to supply demand and reserve requirements.
Technologic methods for reducing peak demands may take several forms. One way is by devices that impose a limit on power taken by a customer. Such devices could be installed on the customer's premises, to operate at some predetermined power level or under control of the utility's load dispatcher.
Rates which incorporate peak-load pricing have been tested extensively in Europe and are in use in a number of European countries. The European experience, however, is not directly transferrable to the U.S. because of differences in electric utility systems, seasonal peaking characteristics and load factors. A major study of time-of-day metering and load management systems by the Edison Electric Institute and the Electric Power Research Institute has been undertaken at the request of the National Association of Regulatory Commissioners (NARUC) 2/. In addition, several studies of rate revision and load management methods are being sponsored by the Federal Energy Administration. Moreover, many regulatory commissions and utilities are studying the potential effects of rate revisions on demands for electric power.
Resolution No. 9 at the Annual Convention of NARUC, San Deigo, California, December 5, 1974.
